reference.source: Standard gynaecology and reproductive surgery texts / international guidance
clinicalPearls: Asherman syndrome is the formation of intrauterine adhesions that partially or completely obliterate the uterine cavity
It classically follows uterine instrumentation, especially curettage after pregnancy loss or postpartum haemorrhage, and sometimes uterine infection or surgery
Typical features are reduced or absent menstruation, cyclical pain from trapped blood, recurrent pregnancy loss, and subfertility
The diagnosis should be considered in a woman with menstrual change or infertility after intrauterine procedures
Hysteroscopy is the reference standard for diagnosis and allows direct visualisation and treatment of adhesions
Saline infusion sonography and hysterosalpingography can demonstrate cavity defects and filling irregularities
Treatment is hysteroscopic division of adhesions with measures to reduce reformation and encourage endometrial regeneration
Outcomes depend on the severity of adhesions and the amount of healthy endometrium remaining
reference.pathophysiology: Asherman syndrome arises when trauma to the basal layer of the endometrium, typically from curettage on a recently pregnant or infected uterus, triggers abnormal healing in which the denuded uterine walls adhere and fibrous adhesions bridge the cavity. Loss of functional endometrium and scarring reduce the responsive tissue available for cyclical growth and shedding, producing hypomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, and can obstruct outflow so that menstrual blood is trapped, causing cyclical pain. Distortion or obliteration of the cavity and impaired endometrial receptivity interfere with implantation and placentation, leading to subfertility, recurrent loss, and later abnormal placentation.
additionalInvestigations: Diagnostic hysteroscopy to visualise and grade adhesions
Hysterosalpingography to assess cavity and tubal patency
Transvaginal ultrasound assessing endometrial thickness and pattern
Hormonal profile to exclude endocrine causes of amenorrhoea
Pregnancy test in any woman with amenorrhoea
redFlags: Cyclical pelvic pain with amenorrhoea suggesting obstructed, trapped menstruation (haematometra)
Recurrent pregnancy loss after uterine instrumentation
Signs of abnormal placentation in a subsequent pregnancy
New amenorrhoea after a recent postpartum or post-abortal procedure
reference.prognosis: Prognosis relates directly to adhesion severity and residual healthy endometrium. Mild adhesions often respond well to hysteroscopic treatment with restoration of menstruation and fertility, while severe, dense scarring with extensive endometrial loss carries a guarded reproductive outlook and a tendency to reform.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in women with menstrual change or infertility after uterine procedures
Attributing amenorrhoea solely to endocrine causes without imaging the cavity
Aggressive or repeated curettage that worsens endometrial damage
Failing to anticipate abnormal placentation in a later pregnancy
references: Standard reproductive surgery and gynaecology texts
management: Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis under direct vision as the definitive treatment to restore the uterine cavity
Post-operative measures to prevent re-adhesion, such as an intrauterine balloon, an intrauterine device or a barrier gel separating the cavity walls
Cyclical oestrogen therapy to promote endometrial regeneration over the treated surfaces
Follow-up hysteroscopy or imaging to confirm cavity restoration and treat any recurrent adhesions
Referral to reproductive medicine for subfertility, with restoration of menstruation and fertility as the goals
Enhanced antenatal surveillance in subsequent pregnancies for abnormal placentation such as placenta accreta and for recurrent loss
Prevention through minimising and gently performing intrauterine instrumentation, especially after pregnancy loss
